opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a really interesting question, and maybe my answer is a little bit different from what people might expect from someone who works on robotics and automation.

The way I see it, education was never really just about acquiring a specific set of skills that you then go and apply in a job. If that were all it was, then sure, you might worry that automation makes it obsolete. But I think the real value of education, especially at the university level, is that it teaches you how to think, how to approach problems you've never seen before, and how to figure out what questions are even worth asking. And those things become more valuable, not less, when the routine parts of work get automated.

If you think about what happens when you have really capable AI systems and robots, the bottleneck shifts. It's no longer "can we execute this task," it's "what should we be doing in the first place, and how do we direct these systems toward things that are actually good and useful." That's a much more open-ended, creative kind of problem, and it requires people who have a broad understanding of the world, who can reason about tradeoffs, who understand a bit of science, a bit of history, a bit of how people work.

I'd also say there's a part of education that's just intrinsically valuable. Understanding how the world works, understanding mathematics, physics, literature, these make life richer. In a world where people potentially have more freedom because a lot of labor is automated, I think that kind of understanding becomes a bigger part of what makes life meaningful.

Now, I do think the form of education will probably change. The idea that you memorize a bunch of facts or learn a bunch of procedures, that's going to matter less, because you'll have tools that do that for you. And honestly, AI tutors could make education dramatically more accessible and personalized. But the core of it, learning to think clearly and deeply, I think that's going to be more important than ever.

r001.rationale: The response says education teaches people how to think, tackle unfamiliar problems, and decide what questions to ask, while memorized facts and procedures matter less. This communicates transferable learning and understanding over imparting particular facts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, partly because I'm a professor and I'm supposed to have an answer. The honest version is that a lot of what we traditionally thought education was for is going to look different, and I think that's fine, because I don't think the main value was ever really the thing it looked like on the surface.

If you think about what a university education does for someone, the superficial reading is that it transfers a body of knowledge. You learn calculus, you learn how to write a compiler, whatever. And that part is clearly the part that automation puts the most pressure on. If you can ask a model to write the compiler, the marginal value of knowing how to write it yourself goes down. I don't want to pretend otherwise.

But I don't think that was ever the deepest thing. When I look at my students, the ones who end up doing really interesting work, the thing they got from their education wasn't a set of facts. It was taste. It was knowing which problems are worth working on, having a sense for when an answer is suspicious even if you can't immediately say why, being able to look at a result and say, that doesn't feel right, let me dig in. That kind of judgment is incredibly hard to acquire without actually struggling with the material yourself. You can't outsource the struggle and still end up with the judgment. And in a world where the systems can generate enormous amounts of plausible stuff very quickly, the ability to evaluate, to decide what's actually good, that becomes more valuable, not less.

There's also a point that's a little more philosophical. In robotics we talk about this a lot, that the hard part is often not the capability but knowing what you want. Specifying the objective. I think as more of the execution gets automated, more and more of what humans actually contribute is going to be on the side of deciding what should be done and why. And education, done well, is really training for that. It's exposure to a lot of ideas, a lot of ways of thinking, so that you have a richer sense of what's possible and what matters.

So I guess my answer is that I think the value of education goes up in some ways, but what we're educating for has to shift. Less about being a repository of knowledge, more about developing the kind of judgment and curiosity that lets you work alongside these systems well. And I'll admit I'm not sure our institutions have fully adjusted to that yet, including the one I work at. But I think the core thing, learning how to think carefully about hard problems, that's going to remain pretty important for a while.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts transmitting facts with developing judgment through struggling with material, evaluating results, and learning to think carefully about hard problems—an equivalent emphasis on building skills and understanding.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish education as preparation for a particular job from education as learning how to understand the world. Automation might change the first one quite substantially, but I don’t think it eliminates the value of the second.

Even if a machine can do a task for you, you still have to decide whether that task is worth doing. What do you want to accomplish? What would a good outcome look like? Those questions require understanding. And often you discover what you want by learning enough about a subject to see what’s possible.

There’s also a potential trap in thinking that, because a system can give you an answer, you no longer need to learn how to get there. Some of the value of working through a difficult problem is that it changes how you think. It gives you intuitions that help you ask better questions later. So I would be cautious about removing all of that work from education.

At the same time, having something that can patiently explain a concept, adapt to what you’re confused about, and let you explore at your own pace could be enormously valuable. The opportunity is to use automation to help people develop more understanding. And that seems worthwhile even in a world where understanding is less directly tied to earning a living.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes learning how to understand the world and how working through problems builds lasting intuitions and better questions, rather than treating education as just receiving answers or facts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think education serves several purposes, and preparing people to do economically valuable work is only one of them. It also gives you the ability to understand the world, to decide what you want, and to ask better questions. Those things remain valuable even if machines can do a lot of the work for you.

Suppose you have a system that can carry out almost any task you give it. You still have to figure out which tasks are worth doing. And you need some basis for evaluating whether the result actually addresses what you care about. You can delegate some of that evaluation, too, but ultimately there’s a question of what you value and what kind of life you want to lead.

I also think there’s something intrinsically rewarding about understanding things. We don’t stop playing chess because computers are better at it. Learning something difficult can be worthwhile even when it doesn’t give you an advantage over a machine.

So I would expect the emphasis of education to change. Perhaps we spend less time preparing people to execute particular procedures, and more time helping them develop understanding, curiosity, and judgment. And automation could make that education much more accessible through individualized instruction. In that sense, the same technology that changes why we learn could also make learning substantially better.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes understanding and judgment over executing procedures, but does not identify education’s value as developing the ability to acquire skills and understanding rather than imparting particular facts.
